utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the Prosecution wanted to raise a preliminary matter. Mr. Traldi, can we deal with it in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not very consistent this morning. We go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dragutinovic. Mr. Dragutinovic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you, but not very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll ask the assistance of the usher to ... Do you now hear -- the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can. I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, before we continue I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. McCloskey will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, going to the subject of the times that you were the duty officer at the Zvornik Brigade, do you recall that General Mladic would fly through Zvornik air-space sometimes in his helicopter?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, but I don't remember any of the details from that time. But the question now is when I was on duty. In what year, during what period of time? I was not on duty that often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just any time that you were duty officer during your service, do you -- did he fly through Zvornik air-space?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know that if he had while you were duty officer, would you have been supposed to register that flight in any records, or for some reason would it not be registered?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, only the announced flights were recorded or entered in the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Only the announced flights. So not the actual flights themselves?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since in the air-space of Zvornik there are not only flights by helicopters of the VRS but also SFOR and UNPROFOR airforce, it is possible that there was a duty officer who did record the actual flights that took place. I don't remember any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's briefly go back to P7152. That's the code cable you -- excuse me, the code table that we had been looking at, and I just want to remind us of a particular code. It's here -- it's number 8. And it says the attack on aerial targets forbidden, and for the period of 11 to 21 July, that code-name would be Cer. And if for translation purposes we wouldn't translate "Cer," we just keep it as "Cer."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So seeing that, let's now go to 65 ter 32119a.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what will be coming up, you'll see, is an operations diary from the Birac Brigade. And of course, I understand you're not from the Birac Brigade, but perhaps you can help us a bit in looking at this. It is a brigade not far from the Zvornik Brigade, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's go to page 2 in both languages. So in this operations diary, we see that there's clearly marked 16 July and some notes about things. Is this consistent with what a duty officer would -- would write down in a brigade, this kind of information?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me to read, I would like to do that. I suppose so. It is actually very hard for me to read here. The document is in handwriting. But in any case, a duty officer should record everything of any importance that happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to a section I do want you to be able to clearly read. That's page 3 in both languages. And if we could look at the entry for 0925 hours, and we see that it says in English: "Zlatar - proceed according to the Grabovica signals table. Cetinje - Evropa - Ruma," and then "Cer until 2030."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in your view, is that consistent with a notification in this diary that attacking -- attacks on aerial targets are forbidden until 2030 hours?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a signal is mentioned and if it comes from the signals table, a table, that really means that fire shouldn't be opened on targets during the time indicated in the signals table. Or if the signals table says that fire should be opened, then the opposite would happen, i.e., fire would be opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we will recall that we had just seen signal Cer in the signals table for 11 through 21 July, and it said "attack on aerial targets forbidden" in the previous exhibit. Now let's go to page 4 of this document, and here we'll see down at 2020 hours a reference that Zlatar, according to the signals table, Grabovica - Cer valid till 22 hours.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that and I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So does this mean that the signal Cer was extended from 2030 hours now to 22 hours?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to see the signals table for Cer, then I would be able to say. It is possible that it was extended until a certain time. Even if a time is set in a signals table, it may always be extended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, in the transcript it reads, line 23, on page 7: "Cer was extended from 2030 hours." In the document itself, it says 2020.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I -- I think there may be some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There may be some confusion. I think the earlier entry we looked made the Cer valid until 2030, and we now see that at 2020 it is extended to 2200 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I thank my Presiding Judge for this explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise for my intervention. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document number 32119a receives number P7153.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7153 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now can we go on the same topic to 65 ter 32124a. And let's -- we see this. This is called the book of the duty officer's observations. It's again from the Birac Brigade. Could we go to page 2. And we see that this is from the duty officer, Lieutenant Jelenko Dzinic and it's dated 16/17 July 1995. It's a report to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I just want to note, draw your attention to under point 1, it's the second paragraph: "At 0935 it was ordered by Zlatar to proceed pursuant to the signal's table Grabovica-Cer till 2200 hours (not shoot at the aircrafts)." Now, that's consistent with the diary entries that we've seen, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we go down to paragraph number 3, it describes: "There were no extraordinary events in the zone of our brigade." Z/o, I take it, is zone of our brigade? "We did not register any flights for" --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of our brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. And then it goes on to say: "We did not register any flights over our territory."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reading that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so based on your experience at the Zvornik Brigade, you've recalled earlier that actual flights may not get registered or not? Does this jog your memory about anything? How would you explain this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the announced flights were entered in the records and that signals table is observed. If that was not done, if the signals table was not complied with, a result would have been undesired consequences. For example, opening fire at an aircraft in our air-space, because you never know what the intention of that aircraft was. In other words, every flight had to be announced because every unit had anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and if General Mladic was flying in his helicopter on the evening hours of 16 July, would it be consistent and wise to have a signal Cer go up to the duty officers in the brigades whose zone air-space he may be flying through or near?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been logical to regulate that by the signals table, i.e., that fire was not opened on any aircraft in the corridor irrespective of the passengers of the aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32124a receives number P7154.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before it will be admitted, Mr. McCloskey, the document reads 16/17th of July. It apparently is an excerpt of a -- of a book. Now, it is a bit unclear, also on the basis of what is at the bottom of the page, "duty handed over," "duty taken over," whether this happened on the 16th, the 17th, et cetera. That's one question. And of course you asked the witness about whether this is consistent with what we find here. Of course, to some extent it is; that is, that Cer was ordered in the morning hours and that it ended at 2200 hours. But, of course, it is not fully consistent as far as chronology is concerned because it was not in the morning hours that it was ordered that Cer would extend until 22 hours. It would be 2030 and was then extended. So to some extent it does, to some extent it does not. At the same time we do not know for sure here, having only this excerpt, whether we are dealing with the 16th, exclusively the 16th, or inclusive the 17th. Do you have any assistance to offer for us to be better able to understand this document in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I have a -- a couple of documents I wasn't -- I wasn't -- well, that I had next in my line and given your concern I best go through them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. That's fine. Because relevance and probative value are the tests for admission, and I do understand that there's still more to come which would satisfy us that the probative value and the relevance is such that it should be admitted. Madam Registrar, you have given the number already. P7154 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I don't have the pages before and after the log-book, but we'll take a look because, as you know, that could help us with your 16/17 July concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- one of the concerns I expressed was that we were dealing with an excerpt that does not answer all the questions that the selected page raises. We'll then wait for you to revisit this aspect. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P1502 at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know if this -- this is a green-covered notebook which we have seen frequently in this case. This is what has been referred to as the Zvornik Brigade duty officer's diary or notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could now go to page 36 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just taking -- well, I know that's hard for you to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps we could blow up the Serbian to give the witness a chance to acclimate to this new document. We see 16 July 1995 noted here and various comments about things that are -- appear to be going on or other issues. So if we can now go to the next page, page 37, and if we can go down to the -- near the bottom, we'll see a notation: "Signal Cer until 2030 hours. At 0926 hours." So I think you've explained that -- about signal Cer until 2030 hours. What does the "at 0926 hours" reference refer to, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see where you see 0906.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, it -- I'll read it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's 0926, I think, and it is the second paragraph from the bottom in B/C/S, Witness. You see -- you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says 0926 here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you take that to mean or be a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, well, I don't really have to get this right. I'm not sure. But it says "signal Cer." Now, I cannot remember the signals table. It was given until, what, 2030? So it was valid until 2030, and the signal was received at 0926.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And while we don't see times noted in some regularity in this document, if we look near the top, we can see that: "Mirko requested link with Maric regarding transfer of food. There was no link between them at 0805." And then at the bottom of the page, we see a reference to some person named "Beara to call Panorama 155 at 0930 hours." So would it be consistent that this duty officer received the signal Cer at 0926 hours and thereby noted it then in the duty book?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in terms of the sequence of these numbers or time references, it would be logical for the signal to be at 9.26 because that is what is written, "at 9.26." So in my view, the signal was received at 9.26. I can just interpret it that way, what you have ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because up here we have 9.22, and then 9.26, and finally we have 9.32, so there is this sequence that tallies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see Beara around your brigade on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th, I was not at the brigade -- or rather, in the area where I could have encountered General or Colonel Beara, I don't know his exact rank, I was on the left flank, so I had no opportunity of seeing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 43 in this document. And without going through each page to sort out precisely what the date may be, I think the Defence will agree that this is still the 16th of July, which should be noted in the duty officer notebook that is in evidence where we have that material noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, we go down near the bottom of the page and it says: "At 2020 hours, the signal Cer was sent from Zlatar, i.e., it's forbidden to shoot at aerial targets until 2200 hours. All units informed about that." Again, is this consistent with the other references we've seen in both Birac and in notebook?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have nothing to add to this. This is put concisely and understandably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. So one last document, if you could help us with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 4340.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a -- what's entitled the provisional telephone directory of the Zvornik Brigade that we picked up from the brigade in a search in 1998, and if I could just show you that it might help you remember it. We've shown that to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In which year was the search carried out, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, does this at all look familiar to you, this little book?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to me. I've never had it in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or I don't remember. I don't think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this the kind of notebook that would hold telephone extensions for the Zvornik Brigade, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a notebook with all the known telephones. Now, whether I remember the booklet itself, and in this form I cannot confirm that for sure, but we have here a phonebook with all the relevant persons and commands, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So could you go just, I think, count about -- it's page 5 in e-court and it's page 7 in the actual book. So just count seven pages and we should get to the Zvornik Brigade command phone numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're page 7 in e-court in English, sorry. It's page 5 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where the transcript tell us that the Chamber conferred, we looked at the original of this document when conferring. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, it was a while back, but I'm sure you had called these phone numbers quite a bit. In fact, we should see your -- do we see the assistant Chief of Staff for operations here?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're looking at the same page, I'll take a look right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the brigade, I mean, this term, I'm not familiar with that, "operations centre."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We also see the Chief of Staff which would have been Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of Staff, all right. Operations centre? Well, we had an operations department where I was assistant Chief of Staff and I had a desk officer. Maybe somebody characterised that as an operations centre. I don't know. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you'd agree with me that your boss was Dragan Obrenovic, the Chief of Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm subordinated to the Chief of Staff because I'm assistant Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see his phone number as -- correct me if I'm wrong, but this is his phone number is it not: 588-556?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, I have to add something. I have to make a remark. Very often numbers changed during the war, depending on the capabilities of the post office and the technical requirements that the postal services could meet, so all of these numbers don't have to be valid from 1993 all the way up until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand. Now, the Chief of Staff's phone number, you'd agree with me, was 588-556, according --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is written here, but I don't remember numbers. I didn't really call very often so that I could remember it. But what is written here is that that is his number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then we see to the right of that, it says 136. That would be his actual phone extension?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be his phone extension, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And do you remember calling that extension? You should have called it occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me way too much. 1993, whether I remember that that was the number, 136. I can tell you that I almost never phoned the extension because my office was right next to that of the Chief of Staff. It was enough for me just to turn around, walk into the office, and get our business done. So this communication via telephone extension, I don't remember. I think I hardly ever used it, if at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go down the list a bit. We see chief of security is number 10. And in July 1995, that would have been who?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago Nikolic was chief of security. I think lieutenant was his rank. Again, whether this is his number, well, according to this, yes. Again, the extension, that's what it should be, but this is from 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If in 1995 Colonel Beara was using Drago Nikolic's office, and we had an intercept which said Beara could be reached at extension 139 -- actually I think I got --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I put the answer in the question. If Beara is at the Zvornik Brigade and we have an intercept that he can be reached at extension 139, would that be consistent with him working out of Drago Nikolic's office, if this is correct and applicable for July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The extension number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is asked to speculate when the question is phrased this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me re-read the question. Well, I think the question is not seeking speculations but rather is seeking that conclusions are drawn on the basis of a certain assumption. Now, if you could rephrase the question in such a way, Mr. McCloskey, that we do not ask the witness to form opinions or draw conclusions. If you are able to establish the facts on which you invite the witness to draw the conclusions, you might even consider to leave it the claim to draw conclusions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If this phone number is valid for July 1995, which it's the position of the Prosecution that it is, and Colonel Beara is said in an intercept -- if an intercept says Colonel Beara can be reached at extension 139, would that be consistent with Colonel Beara working out of Drago Nikolic's office?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was this question put to me? Since I absolutely do not remember any of these numbers, it is logical that I wouldn't remember that now, I don't remember this number, I don't remember the telephone directory. Mr. Beara, I did not come across him. So I'm not going to say specifically whether Mr. Beara called from this number because I do not know. As for a conclusion, it can be made by anyone who can base it on this answer of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In that event I would seek agreement with my colleague, Mr. Stojanovic, that this document be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not opposed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document with number 04340 receives number P7155.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7155 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, that is -- I am -- I am finished, and I went over my time a bit, but I had not originally planned to go into the Zvornik Brigade signal Cer documents, but I think it was a good idea that we did and so that is a bit of my extra time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could I, while we're here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We prefer to hear from you before you take the extra time that you want to stray away from what apparently was on your mind to start with and then that you seek permission to do so, but let's leave it to that. That's what we expect the Defence to do as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, while I'm still here, I would like to also offer in the Defence's witness statement which was 1D01643 which we spent a bit of time dealing with, and it's short, but I think given the history of this and the interest it should go in. In addition, there's a brief proofing note that was designed to help correct it, which is 65 ter 32122 -- excuse me, 32123, which I think should go with it as they go together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For what purpose do you tend -- do you tender this in order to enable the Chamber to better assess the reliability and credibility of this witness? Is that the purpose? Or is it for the truth of its contents, because you would have to seek attestations?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's to help explain the testimony and the references to the questions. It would just be so much easier when looking into this that -- that you had in front of you. But I -- so I would like you to be able to take full awareness of it, be it truth or be it lie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But also to rely on it for the truth of its content?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, not that it's necessarily true. As I've argued many times, sometimes a document with a lie is very revealing. So you're in the best position to sort it out. I would like you to be able have to it fully and not have any limited purpose to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since my understanding was that the proofing note is being tendered as well, the one through which I informed the Prosecution and the Chamber about the corrections that the witness gave to us in paragraph 13, in that case, we are not going to oppose having his statement admitted, along with paragraph 13 changes. We don't have that problem then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, we need two numbers: One for the statement of the witness, the other one for the proofing note.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statement currently bearing number 1D01643 will receive number P7156.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the proofing note would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Proofing note with number 32123 will receive number P7157.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7156 and P7157 are admitted into evidence. You've done with your cross-examination, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think it would be wisest to take the break. Mr. Stojanovic, could you tell us how much more time you would need in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between 10 and 13 minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then the average would be 11 and a half, but you have a quarter of an hour after the break. We take the break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Witness, and you will be soon --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- released after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, you'll now be re-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I would like to call up P7148.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And while we're waiting for that to appear on the screen, let me tell you, Mr. Dragutinovic, that the document is actually the map that you saw yesterday and where you marked the facilities at Viogor and Suceska.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask the assistance of the usher who will give you a pen, and I'm going to ask you to mark the Zepa axis as the crow flies from Viogor; in other words, where is Zepa in respect of that circle that you used to mark Viogor. Can you put an arrow there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we use a pen of a different colour, I would suggest, but it's done already. We have now a green pen being used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, green.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next thing I wish to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this stay on the screen for the time being, and then I will ask for it to be marked. Just for the record, I would like to say that the witness used a green pen to draw an arrow showing the Zepa direction in respect of the Viogor sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now, Witness, yesterday you spoke about the reactions of members of TG 1 [as interpreted], i.e., Combat Group 2, when they learned that they would be ordered to continue moving towards Zepa. That's on page 70, line 4, through page 71, line 7. To the best of your recollection, when did that reaction happen?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned together with the commander of the tactical group into the sector of the TG, the commander --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please slow down so that all your words will be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We organised a short briefing about the situation in the units as well as the possible use of those units. During that briefing, the commander of TG 2 or, rather, Combat Group 2, presented the situation as it was in the unit at the time. He literally said that the unit was not fit for combat because previously it had had seven fallen soldiers and three wounded and about 13 missing in action. It was a huge loss for a company that had a total of 120 men. Before that, the commander of the TG emphasised that it was possible to use units of the Zvornik Brigade in the Zepa sector, and I underline the word "possible."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the morning when the commander arrived from the Zeleni Jadar sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you something else with regard to this map. You are one of the authors of the map, and you said that during the cross-examination. I would like you to tell the Trial Chamber when this map was actually drafted, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just an excerpt from a rather bigger map, just a segment of a bigger map, so I can't really say when it was drafted. However, it is linked to the activities surrounding Srebrenica. I can't remember the date. In practical terms, this is a working map. And when it comes to the events surrounding combat activities in Srebrenica, those events were entered in the topographical maps to accompany every order for every unit, and that was something that the commander of every TG had to have on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As the assistant Chief of Staff for operations and training, until the end of the war, until the moment you were demobilised, did you have access to the documents of the Zvornik Brigade, including all these maps?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the maps and all the documents of the Zvornik Brigade were kept in the operations and training department. I was the head of that department. All the maps which were kept in the operations and training department were authored either by me personally or by my assistants, and they are part of the documentation of the Zvornik Brigade. All the documents that existed in the Zvornik Brigade were produced in the operations and training department. At the end of the war, all the documents were archived, packed neatly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please slow down again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. [Interpretation] All the documents were collected, archived, and prepared to be handed over to the corps command. That was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you were requested by anybody or when you were ordered by anybody to change any of the documents, to forge any of the documents, to add something to them, or correct any of the documents in any way?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the documents which were kept in my department are original, and they were all intended to be archived by the corps command without any alterations or additions being made to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now tell me, speaking from your professional experience, in the brigade, as a rule, when would the duty officer's duty start and when it ended?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What duty do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The operative duty of the duty operations officer in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you the exact time, but it was ongoing; it was constant. The duty operations officer had his assistant. When a higher-ranking officer was appointed as the duty operations officer, he was replaced by his assistant during the night. And then in the morning, it would be higher-ranking officers, who then handed over the duty to his successor for the following day. There were always two men: The duty operations officer and his assistant. I really can't remember the exact time when their duty started or ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, how long was an officer on duty for?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the whole of 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the period of 24 hours, was that how much time one of the two officers spent on duty?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of the command members was always on duty for 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now let me finish with the following question. You were shown several documents relative to the signals tables and signals records. Speaking from your experience, please tell us whether you know that there was situations that a flight would be announced through the signals table and that that flight never happened.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened. Not once; many times. For various reasons. Flights were delayed, and then signals would be altered so as to indicate that a flight would not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I will end with another question. With regard to your job, do you know that in the air-space of the Zvornik Brigade there were helicopter flights or UNPROFOR flights carrying humanitarian aid, all that in the area controlled by the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR helicopters and helicopters of other humanitarian organisations often flew over the area controlled by the Zvornik Brigade. That was one of their flight corridors when they flew from Belgrade to Sarajevo or in some other direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the signals table that we spoke about, would it also be functioning when you had UNPROFOR flights?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it applied to UNPROFOR flights as well because it was very difficult to identify an aircraft visually and say who it belonged to. In other words, all flights had to be monitored and had to be announced through the signals table.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, thank you on behalf of General Mladic's Defence and the general himself for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this brings my re-examination to an end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you stayed well within your time estimates. May I take it that you want to tender the newly marked map or would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the map now marked with a green arrow in addition to previous markings would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be D915, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. We now get something very special on our screens. Well, I don't know what it stands for or whether it's some training exercise done. It has now disappeared from our screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just on this UNPROFOR flight. Should be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Further cross-examination by Mr. McCloskey:

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you just answered a question about UNPROFOR flying over RS air-space. In this case, the -- the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that about on I believe it's between 8 July and 11 July, when you were in Srebrenica, that a -- a Dutch soldier was killed and the UN requested an air-lift via helicopter to pick up his body, and that was declined. The evidence is that that was declined initially. I just ask you that would you know that when UNPROFOR is flying helicopters over RS air-space, they have to get permission to do that; don't they?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG DRAGUTINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they should. They should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dragutinovic, this concludes your evidence. I'd like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe return home again, and you may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are, Your Honour. We are calling Mr. Krcmar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, we've looked at the log-book that the date concerns, and it looks like two or three pages on either side help identify the concern. So we'll be back, after speaking to the Defence, hopefully with an agreement on which pages. And if I would -- and Ms. Melikian would leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Mr. Traldi remains, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who will lead the witness? You, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I had some questions. If looking at paragraphs -- well, let's say around the 50, there are a lot of photographs and short statements. Apparently, the photographs are at least to some extent taken also from web sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is all kind of comment on it. It remains, however, totally unclear where the knowledge of the witness comes from in relation to this material. For example, if he says, "Here you see a photograph of -- of small children diseased," I've got no idea whether the witness can tell us anything about whether these were children that died at birth or in hospital or that they were killed in any other way. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My intention is to go through even some of the associated exhibits, since they are actually -- associated exhibits are actually pictures from the statement only enlarged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. But in the statement as it appears now, there was not much explanation of it and it may be difficult to understand what exactly the witness adds to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krcmar. Before you give evidence, the Rules require --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krcmar, although the text is well known to our interpreters, you spoke so quickly that they even had already difficulties in interpreting those words. Could you please try to adapt your speed of speech so that everything will be interpreted and that we're not missing any of your words. You'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. You will find Mr. Lukic to your left. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you, but I just want to ask you one thing before I start. I asked for additional time. Is it granted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think you couldn't do without for -- and, again, you asked for how much?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For two and a half hours in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two and a half hours. I think in view of what we see before us, and also keeping in mind that, of course, it's for you to decide how you want to use your 207 and a half hours, that the Chamber does not oppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just kindly ask the usher --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Prosecution also asked for two and a half hours for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Thank you. If I kindly ask the usher to give the witness his statement in hard copy, please. It's checked by the Prosecution. And if -- yeah. And if we can have on our screens 1D1744, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krcmar, good morning.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us your name for the record. Slowly.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: My name is Goran Krcmar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krcmar, did you give a statement to the Defence of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before you on the screen, and you also have it in hard copy, is the first page. Do you recognise the signature on this first page of the document?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could we display the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have it on the screen now. Do you recognise the signature on this page? Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is also my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to go to the penultimate page in both versions; paragraph 52, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will remember, I'm sure, that we discussed the number of statements you provided to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes. So far, I have provided three statements to the OTP in the Delic case. I said that I gave just one statement, because I thought that all three were one and the same, because they were about the same case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I will just read the first sentence of paragraph 52, and it reads: "Prior to this, I gave a statement to the ICTY Office of the Prosecutor in the case against Rasim Delic, on 6 October 2007." After the explanation, we deem it proper that this sentence of paragraph 52 should read, I quote: "Prior to this, I gave three statements to the ICTY Office of the Prosecutor in the case against Rasim Delic on 21st December 2005, 6 June 2007, and on 6th October 2007."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then you should adapt the next sentence as well. Then you should say the last statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can redact that sentence since I don't have all ERN numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear that the reference to the ERN is not valid any further. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having made this correction, Mr. Krcmar, would you say that what is recorded in the statement has been recorded well and reflects what you told the Mladic Defence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what you told us and what has been recorded in the statement, is it true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes, everything is true and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you answer them in the same way?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would tender this statement into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D1744 receives number D916.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will read summary statement -- actually, statement summary that is not that short. It will be a bit longer than usual. And then I will have several questions, with your leave, Your Honours, for this witness. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In the beginning of the war, Mr. Krcmar was mobilised into the Army of Republika Srpska, and in April 1993 he was appointed by the command of the 1st Krajina Corps as a member of the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War of the 1st Krajina Corps. He performed this duty until April 1996 when military commissions stopped operating and the government of Republika Srpska made a decision to establish the State Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners of War and Missing Persons. Each corps of the Army of Republika Srpska had its exchange commission. The VRS military commissions dealt exclusively with the examination of prisoners of war and bodies of perished VRS soldiers. Mr. Krcmar will explain the manner of establishing contact with the opposite side, as well as the locations of military prisons in the zone of 1st Krajina Corps. Mr. Krcmar will testify that the ICRC representatives were allowed to access the military prisons of VRS and register the prisoners of war, unlike the prisons on the side of the Army of B and H, where it was not allowed until sometime in 1994, when the first Serb prisoners of war were registered in the ABiH prisons. The Serb side constantly had fewer prisoners than was the case with the other sides to the conflict, and it created large problems for his commission when they negotiated the exchange, bearing in mind that exchanges were agreed based on the one-for-one principle. The reason for such a situation - the lack of enemy prisoners of war - was, inter alia, the fact that the VRS acted defensively during the war and it had no opportunity to capture enemy soldiers. Mr. Krcmar will testify about beatings and torture and there were cases of prisoners succumbing to the injuries caused by the beatings in the ABiH-controlled prisons. He will testify about killings of Serbs in B and H captivity. Mr. Krcmar will testify that today there is no official register of either killed or missing persons due to the obstruction by the institutions of the Federation of B and H and the institutions at the level of B and H, such as the B and H Missing Persons Institute. The Muslim/Bosniak side does not want a central register of the missing persons to be established in B and H, although there is a the Law on Missing Persons at the level of B and H which, inter alia, envisaged the establishment of the central register of the missing persons by the end of 2008. Mr. Krcmar will testify about the manipulation with the number of killed and missing Muslims/Bosniak. The names of missing Muslims/Bosniaks have never been published save for the numerical data that have been proven incorrect through a number of analyses. Mr. Krcmar will explain the difference between the actually missing Muslim, having their name and surname, and the exaggerated number that is not covered by names is secured through a so-called cases. In this manner, the numbers of Bosniaks/Muslim victims are manipulated, the exaggerated figures of non-existing and nameless victims are covered, and a false picture is created about the missing persons in B and H. And that's the end of statement summary. And with your leave, Your Honours, I will have quite a bit questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krcmar, how long have you been involved in this issue, i.e., searching for missing people?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: When it comes to searching for missing people, I've been involved in that since April 1993. Because the job is not completed, so I'm involved in that still.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are the missing persons and the detainees being searched for even after the end?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: The deadline to release all prisoners of war was 28th of January, 1996. Republika Srpska honoured the deadline and freed all its prisoners of war. However, that was not reciprocated by the Federation and there were still people in the prisons under the control of the BH army. We knew the Muslim side was still hiding Serbian prisoners of war. For that reason, we addressed the High Commissioner to visit General Sakib Mahmuljin, the commander of the 3rd Corps of the BiH army, because we knew that in the area of his responsibility there were still some hidden prisoners of war. Sometime in 1996 we organised that meeting, and I and another colleague of mine met with the commander Sakib Mahmuljin. On that occasion Mahmuljin told me that he knew nothing about any prisoners of war, that he had honoured all the procedures, that all the prisoners of war had been liberated, which was not true because in one camp alone run by El Mujahid Brigade, there were 63 Serbian prisoners. And also in Zenica, we knew for a fact that there were two prisoners of war there. They were officers of the VRS. Their names were Skrbic and Skrbic. We could not come to terms with such a statement on his part. We continued searching. And then in 1998, three years after the end of the war, three years after the end of the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could well be, Mr. Lukic, that the witness is exactly telling you what you wished to hear without even having asked the witness. The witness comes with a long story, where the question was rather short. Could you please, in order to avoid that in one or two days from now, that we have to end up in saying that we need far more time, to keep firm control over what evidence you want to elicit from this witness, and rather than to let him go in every direction. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please just finish the sentence that you started.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: In 1998 the IPTF found two Serb captives, Skrbic and Skrbic, at the prison in Zenica. They were hidden and were not registered by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 13 of your statement, you say that the exchange agreed upon was one-for-one. Were there any proposals to have exchanges all-for-all?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes. In all our talks with the other side we proposed that, because we had instructions from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska to insist on that kind of exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to show a film, a documentary film, and then I'm going to ask you something about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Lukic, may I take it that the film is not there to lead the witness, because otherwise you would have to first ask the question and then show the film. But -- I don't know what questions you have in relation to that film, but there's always a risk of being extremely leading if you first show pictures and then ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly what you know about the film that is called "Kiss Thy Brother"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: It contains statements of survivors from El Mujahid and Gostovici. Also, the film contains material that was filmed by the members of the El Mujahid unit and that it was in the hands of the MUP of Republika Srpska. The film was made at the request of camp inmates of Republika Srpska. That is their film and I participated at their request.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are again invited to speak more slowly. So I do understand that the film is produced with your assistance and your involvement. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you take part in the liberation of the people who are speaking in this film?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly how that came about, how they were freed? And then we will continue.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: The people who are making statements in this film were freed on the 26th of January, 1996, when all other POWs were freed too. So it was not an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We stopped here in this video material 1 minute, 51 seconds, and now I would kindly ask that we move on to 1 minute, 54 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do that, Mr. Lukic, can I just get clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, how did you get hold of the material that had been filmed by the El Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That material is in the possession of the MUP of Republika Srpska. Also a great deal of video material that they themselves filmed were being circulated there Bosnia-Herzegovina and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I know it is in the custody of the -- as you say, in the custody of the Republika Srpska. My question is how did you get hold of it? How did it get into the hands of the Republika Srpska; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This material is in the archives of the Federation of camp inmates of Republika Srpska. I did not get a hold of it. I just took part in this. But the statements that are being made are made by people who live to this day in Republika Srpska, who are survivors of these camps, and one person appeared before this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me stop you. Let me stop you again. My question really was do you know how the Republika Srpska got hold of the material? If do you know, just say I know, this is how it happened; or if you don't know, just say I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can say that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we see what is went on the screen here, "Kiss Thy Brother." Is that the film that you've been speaking about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we continue now, please. And we will go up to 3 minutes and 10 seconds. And we start from 2 minutes, 3 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we stop, please. I don't know how this would work. We provided the booths with the translation and B/C/S versions. So it should be translated and it's checked by CLSS, Your Honours, I just want to inform you that it was checked, and actually revised translation is uploaded into the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you have provided the booth with the original transcript and the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the transcript. If that is the case, I think that we could play it. If it has been verified that the transcript is accurate compared to what is said on the video and then we would receive -- look at the video and we receive in both languages -- or at least the original, of course, will be heard directly, whereas we will receive the English translation. That's how I understand it will go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, okay, you give the instructions as where to start, and I take it that that then should be clear to the booth as well. We started with some music, I think, which is not in need of any translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was some speech by the speaker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can start at 2:04.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] the Mujahedin commander gives the final instructions to his brothers before the action. They are joyful because the encounter with the Serbs will come soon and because they have been chosen to be in the front ranks. Preparations are complete and they are going towards their destination. After the morning prayer, the Mujahedin will strike against the Serbian fortifications."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We should move to 2 minutes, 55 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment, we hear something but we don't see anything. But that is now apparently being ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you know this part of the film that has letters in Arabic on it? Is that the film that was captured from the Mujahedin or is that something that was recorded by the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: The information that I had is that this was received from the Mujahedin and that it is the Mujahedin that had recorded this. The Serb side did not have that possibility at the time to be there on the spot and to record this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, to interrupt. I'd understood the description that this was a video prepared by the RS association of camp inmates. This appears to have been filmed by someone completely different, and so now I have some uncertainty as to what the representation is as to what exactly we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it was my understanding that this may be part of a film which is produced and in which there were certain portions embedded which were filmed by the Mujahedin. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have only seen those parts yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll further look at what you will present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can now look at segment number 2. It's -- it goes from 8 minutes, 50 seconds, and we will play it up to 11 minutes, 47 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We stopped, actually, at -- you have -- I don't have numbers. You have to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] They counted six people and they said that that's six of them slaughtered." "I did not see all of this: Jankovic, Radonjic, Nikic. "I remained alone on a tree stump, and they came there to see the Chetnik, and they spat at me and did all sorts of things to me. "One screamed when they killed him and I did not ... they took a hammer and smashed his head and I heard them shouting it's a hard head. Then I heard bones breaking. I was a few metres away when I clearly heard the sound of bones breaking. "I was convinced when they saw that this was the command and they found everyone who was supposed to be there, that they would kill us all. "I saw them cut off a head and hold it up like this. "See how their lord has punished and humiliated them."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krcmar, how many Serbs were taken prisoner by the Mujahedin or, rather, the 3rd Corps, do you know, in these operations at Ozren?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: In three operations - in May 1995, in July 1995, and on the 10th of September, 1995 - about 180 Serbs went missing and were taken prisoner by the El Mujahedin Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We saw at the beginning of this segment live Serbs who had been taken prisoner. Do you know how many Serbs survived out of those who were taken prisoner by the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Only eight persons saved, and they were set free.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was taken prisoner when? Were they all taken prisoner at the same time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: I freed these people, and I know Velibor Pribicevic. He was from the medical corps. He was taken prisoner on the 21st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot follow at this pace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, again if you don't slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are speaking very fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you don't slow down, your testimony will be lost which we would not wish to happen. So please speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll start from the beginning, Velibor Pribicevic, taken prison on the 21st of July, 1995, at Paljenik, municipality Zavidovic, Mount Ozren. On the same day, Vinko Aksentic was taken prisoner and another witness who will appear here. His name is Igor Buljevati. Nuhanovic, Novica, who described the slaughter and the position how the Mujahedin is holding this head, he was taken prisoner on the 10th of September, 1995 at Mount Ozren, municipality of Zavidovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let us take a look at the third segment. Let's just say that we stopped at 11 minutes, 47, as far as the second segment is concerned. And now we should start at 13 minutes, 1 second, and it should go up until 17 minutes, 49 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] When we reached the line, there was a corpse up there near the first trench, and it had a hole made by a pickax that was lying next to the corpse. The hole in the upper part of the chest was the size of a cup, and the head was severed and about 20 centimetres away from the corpse. They lay me in that sand or gravel and hit me with whatever came to hand, punching, kicking me, and hitting me with rifles and everything they had. "They ran and brought axes, meat cleavers, pickaxes, the lot, and stuck them in the sand in front of my eyes. They drew swords across the throat to show how they would slaughter us. They shouted Allahu Akbar and stuck the axe into the ground in front of the eyes so that it sprayed up. That man lay dead. And so they put me and someone there. They really took it out on us, sat on our necks, pulled them back, and I don't know what else. All that remained to be done was to clear the area of Serbs who had not managed to escape. "The Mujahedin have entered the gates of Moscow. The road from Ozren to Vozud [phoen] has fallen under the control of infantry weapons. Anyone who does not believe in Jahannam will be banished so that Allah can separate the good from bad and pile the bad on top of each other and cast them all into hell. They shall indeed be lost. "Tell the non-believers that if they repent they will be forgiven their past sins, but if they do not repent it is well known what happened to ancient peoples. Jihad is truly a constant action that destroys all obstacles in its way and burns all the trenches of Allah's enemies. The enemies of Allah have been killed, made prisoner, or have fled. This is their end in this world and they await painful suffering on judgement day."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was just informed that we had to stop at 15:50 and now we will continue at 17:33 up to 17:49, and I will then have some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for the break, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whatever you prefer. We can break here as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I would invite the parties to think about what the relevance and the probative value of this is, and whether there's dispute that cruelties of the most horrible kind were committed not only as charged by the Serb sides but that similar cruelties were committed by the other side as well. Because if there's no dispute about that, Mr. Traldi, apart from whether we know exactly what it all depicts, whether it is footage taken in this period of time in that area, but -- Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If I could have just a second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have the whole of the break to consider it. And this question does not come as a -- should not come as a surprise because the issue came to the mind of the Judges when reading the statement already. And of course, we are not going to repeat the tu quoque discussion because we know what the Defence thinks about that. But whether these details are related to a matter which is generally in dispute, we'd like to hear from the Prosecution after the break. Witness, you -- we'll take a break, and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at a quarter past 12.00. No loud speaking by Mr. Mladic. We resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just to respond to your question before the break, the Prosecution does not dispute that crimes, including serious violations of international criminal law, were committed by all three sides to the conflict. The Prosecution notes in this regard that Mr. Krcmar has testified about some of those crimes as a Prosecution case in a case at this Tribunal where the accused was charged with crimes in municipalities, including Zavidovici. Based on what we saw from the video, I couldn't tell if it was exactly the same incident or anything, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you do not exclude like depicted, I'm not saying the ones depicted, to have been committed in that context?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We don't exclude cruelties to have been committed among the crimes, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we -- then, Mr. Lukic, having heard what the Prosecution says, there's no dispute about that, that crimes were committed by all sides and that cruelties like you've shown them -- and we didn't stop you. We looked at it for a while, and we thought it wiser not to immediately raise the question as to whether it was in dispute or not and to let you show it. This is a public trial. To let you show that. Although we do not know yet exactly whether this was part of what happened in this war, but we let you go there for a while, and we'd like now to go back to what is the core of this case, and that is, whether the crimes as charged were committed, yes or no. Would you please keep that in mind in the continuation of your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will reorganise. I will have to show several more segments from this movie to this witness, and I can ask hem whether he knows that these photos are from that area and from the period of time we are discussing here in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even that is relatively irrelevant because it's not in dispute that they may be. So therefore, that's why I explicitly asked Mr. Traldi whether when he says there's no issue about crimes having been committed on all sides, why I asked him whether that would include cruelties such as, and he said he doesn't exclude that. So therefore we can work on the basis of the assumption that such cruelties were committed against Serbs. Therefore, there's no dispute about that. Unless there is any specific link you would like to make between what we see and what then happened after that; for example, if one of the victims then later did something, then, of course, we'd like to know that; but only if there is a concrete and explicit link. The general issue is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- agreed upon, I would say. So, therefore, please be very careful in -- again, spending time, especially if it's a lot of time, on issues which are not in dispute. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krcmar, we'll shorten things a bit. I will not be showing the entire video, but let me ask you whether you knew that women and children were also members of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes, I knew about that, and the source of my knowledge were my after-war conversations with my associates, Muslims who hail from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we're going to look at segment 5 in the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi is on his feet. And I missed not only on the transcript but also in the translation what you said when you said let me ask you whether you knew that, and then there's a --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Women and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Women and children --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- were also members of the -- women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I was just going to request, the witness referred to Muslims from the area, if it could be clarified with him which area he is referring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps who they were. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic, and please first deal with the matter raised by Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When I said in this area, I meant Bosnia-Herzegovina and the BiH army. Did you hear that in Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, in its army, there were also women and children who were members of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was: What area are you talking about? Because you earlier said that you heard that from Muslims in your area. What's that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The area around Ozren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The area around Ozren. Who did you speak to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the war, I co-operated with the local Muslims from Zavidovici, Banovici, Maglaj. In my conversations with them, I learnt about the graveyards of the missing persons as well as of who members of the BiH army were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have names of your sources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a matter of principle, I do not name people in order to protect them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, may I be very clear to you: Whether or not there's any need to protect anyone is for this Chamber to decide. You are under an obligation to answer any question that is put to you. And I immediately add to that, that if you consider that there are reasons to give those names in private session, you may address me.
