Do you want to give those names rather in private session than in public session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. My question was whether you would prefer to give those names, which I asked you for, in private session or in public session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the names, not directly. And that's why I'm requesting time to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you don't know the names, that's fine. We accept that. There's no need to -- to explain that. What you do not know, you cannot tell us. But you said: I don't give names as a matter of -- in order to protect persons. You didn't say, I don't know the names, which would have avoided this whole discussion and this waste of time. Then what did they tell you exactly about numbers of women and children being members of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I never insist on people giving me their names, if they're my sources of information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness. Witness, you are continuing a discussion which is concluded. Could you please answer my question: What they said exactly about numbers of women and children being members of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of any numbers, but I know that they participated in the war, that there were children in the BiH army, and that there were even women. I know that. I know as much. But I don't remember the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Children of what age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 16 years, to be very specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 16 years. No information about numbers. Any information about functions? For example, functions held by the women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could play this fifth segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] In the same way as Mujahedin and their women are being trained, so are their children who are their hope for the future in the struggle against the infidel. This boy before you is continuing along the path of his father who was one of the first Mujahedin and whose life was ended on the slopes of Sarajevo about three years ago."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now going to skip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But even now, Mr. Lukic, could the witness tell us: Do you know the footage we saw which was somewhere outside persons where that was and when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was recorded in 1995. The location is Gostovici in Zavidovici municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what's your source knowledge that this stems from that area and from that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All will be revealed as the recording or the footage continues. I recognise the locations where the footage was recorded because I'd been there personally on my own and also accompanied by the investigators of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, please keep in the back of your mind the earlier guidance that we need specific links between what is shown on the footage and what happened after that in order to make it of sufficient relevance to show it and to make it of sufficient probative value. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can start this video at 1 hour, 4 minutes, 51 seconds. It is about the visit of Mr. Izetbegovic to this camp from --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] State of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Supreme Command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina have recognised the El Jihad unit as an independent unit of the army under its command." "So the helicopter landed in the camp. I can't say who was coming. "When they took me into detention, Alija Izetbegovic came immediately the next day. "I didn't see anyone. I didn't hear anything specific so I can't say he was there or someone else. "They said our president was here. "I heard them saying Alija, Alija, Alija. "I found out later that Alija was there to see for himself how it was and what was what."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have -- just have to see -- we have to skip one segment. Now we'll see from 1 hour, 6 minutes, 32 seconds, to 1 hour, 7 minutes, 25 seconds. We can start.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krcmar, do you recognise the location where we saw the tents and the houses?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes. The location is Gostovic and it is the Ristovic family household.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of the Ristovic family?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Let me correct myself. Their name was Ristic and they are of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that area before the war, who were the inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: The inhabitants of that area were Serbs. There's a Serbian monastery there dating back to the 16th century.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How come that you recognise this place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: As I was searching for the missing prisoners of war who were depicted in this footage, on several occasions I went to this location together with the Ristic family members as well as with the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, just as I told you a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now we're going to see a short segment starting at 1:06:16 until 1:06:31. I'm just going to ask you whether you recognise the men in the segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] We were a unit, a lawful unit of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, part of the army, and he was our leader, the president of this state, and we had contact with him like all the other units, you know."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I again inquire whether this dispute -- I -- I -- although I'm not certain, Mr. Lukic, I feel that you want to establish that there were Mujahid Units incorporated in the BiH army and that they considered to be under the final command of Mr. Izetbegovic. My question then is whether there's dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there isn't a dispute that some such units were present and participated in the conflict. I am afraid I'm not able to speak to the formal matter of incorporation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So the presence and -- of Mujahid Units, apart from their very formal status, is not in dispute. Mr. Lukic, so therefore there's no need to -- perhaps the -- having Mr. Izetbegovic there may shed some additional light on it, not on the presence but perhaps on how he considered -- what he considered to be the place of those troops and perhaps on what those troops thought Mr. Izetbegovic was in relation to them. That's apparently an issue which is not -- so therefore, no problem if you present that, but all the rest is -- is not needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want Mr. Krcmar to, if he can recognise this man who's talking to us, and then we'll later on establish further relationships.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've seen him. Perhaps Mr. Krcmar could immediately -- could immediately answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was an officer in the 3rd Corps of the BiH army. He was also the commander of the El Mujahid Brigade detachment that was part of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His name is Abu Hamza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he hails from Bosnia-Herzegovina or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: No. He hails from an Arabic country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which one, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know it directly. But I know that he is currently in detention, in an asylum detention unit, and that he was ordered to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's, then, the source of your knowledge that he is from an Arabic country, if you don't know from which country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all the members of the El Mujahid Brigade come from one of the Arabic states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the -- it's -- it's, rather, a general knowledge or a conclusion rather than specific knowledge about this person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I don't know about him directly, what country he is from; but in principle, all of them are from that part of the world, from an Arabic state, one or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] In these attacks on the 10th of September" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to say when do we start. We start at 1 hour, 31 minutes, 8 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it looks as if our witness is speaking in the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] In these attacks on the 10th of September, 1995, 668 soldiers of the Army of Republika Srpska went missing, most of them members of the 4th Ozren, 2nd Ozren, and 3rd Ozren Brigades, the 14th Serbian Brigade, which comprised units such as the 16th and the 2nd Krajina Brigade, the OKB, the Teslic, Mrkonjic, and other units."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I played this just to show that you were depicted in this video-clip. You gave us some numbers. And after that, we will see Dr. Zeljko Karan speaking. What was his role in the effort to find all those who went missing in Ozren?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: He is a forensic expert, a pathologist. All the bodies who were found anywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina, not only in Ozren, were actually examined by him. The post-mortems of those bodies were done by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to play the part where you're speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Lukic repeat the time reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1 hour, 32 minutes, 19 seconds, up to 1 hour, 32 minutes, 38 seconds. It's very hard to adjust. It's easier maybe to play all the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] So 208 people were exchanged. We don't know what happened to 460 others. And so of those 460 people, only two have had luck to survive. These were people who had been literally abducted from the Zenica KPD in 1998."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krcmar, you're referring to 208 people. They were exchanged. When were they exchanged?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: One group was exchanged on the -- or, rather, set free on the 27th of January, 1996, whereas the other group, some 137 or 138 people all in all, were set free only in April 1996. They had been kept in the prison in Tuzla even after the deadline envisaged by the Dayton Accord had expired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about the 460 people?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: When it comes to those 460 people, at that moment nobody knew what had happened to them. They were still considered missing. Only two were found alive in Zenica. We are still searching for 136 who went missing on Mount Ozren. The rest had already been located, identified, and handed over to their families who then buried them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the war, did you go on field missions to the area where the Mujahedin camp had been set up looking for these people?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes. The first time I went to that location was sometime in September 1997. It's Gostovici. The logistics, the case of the El Mujahid Brigade. At that time there weren't any tents there, but the contours on the ground were quite clear where one could see where it was that the tents were placed. We took photographs. We reconstructed all of that. And we saw the situation in 1997 and realised that was that location and the houses that can be seen there. The Ristic family recognised their houses.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you find anything at that location?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: At the location of Gostovici, we did not find a single body on that occasion. We just learnt where the mass grave was with the bodies of 64 Serbs who were killed at the El Mujahid camp. It is called Kucice. It is 4 kilometres away from Zavidovici towards Gostovic. When we arrived at the location, there were no bodies there. And we saw this area, 10 by 10 metres, roughly, that had been dug out, and there was no soil there, no nothing. The depth was about 1.30. And the bodies were moved in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, same question, Mr. Traldi. Is it in dispute that persons were found in mass graves, dead persons that may have been killed by -- in Mujahedin camps or close to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honour, the more -- the very specific proposition, I would need a little bit of time to speak to. The proposition that Serb victims of some of the crimes that I'd noted earlier were found in mass graves certainly is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I take it that you'll not only skip some of your videos but you'll shorten your time as well, because apparently you had all kind of other things on your mind --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm done with the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I had a lot to play, but in the light of the answers we received from Mr. Traldi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I took it that the two and a half hours you asked for, that that was including showing all that material, so you must have quite some time left now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you went out into that terrain, were you allowed to work unhindered?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: We work -- we had agreed with the commission that we could work in the area of the Federation along parallel lines as they worked in the territory of Republika Srpska, but there were quite a few problems involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were at Ozren with Dr. Karan --

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes, we went out into the field together. We worked together on all the exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were at Paljenik. The film would have shown that had we played it. Could you tell us briefly what happened at Paljenik? Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: During 1997, we worked on the sanitisation of the area; that is to say, we collected the bodies, the mortal remains there. Our entire team was at this feature called Paljenik. We found eight bodies and we prepared them for transportation. We had IFOR together with us, also the police of the Federation, and the commission of the Federation. At one moment we were threatened and told that we had to leave that location within 15 minutes because the road that we had taken on our way there had been blocked by people from Srebrenica. When I say "Srebrenica," may I just explain. In 1996, it is precisely these Serb villages that had been populated by people who had fled from Srebrenica. We withdrew from the location without the body of -- carrying out the bodies, the tools, anything. After a few interventions with IPTF and the Office of the High Representative, again we were enabled to go out into the field and to collect the bodies. When we arrived there, we found a horrible situation. The bodies that had been prepared for transportation had been burned on the stake and one body was on a stretcher by the road. We, the Serb delegation, came to that location, while our colleagues from the federal commission and the police of the Federation did not come with us. They stayed about 500 metres, perhaps, behind our backs. We found that to be suspicious, why this one body was on the stretcher. Since we hadn't left it that way, we asked for deminers to intervene, and underneath that stretcher the sappers realised that there was a land-mine, and underneath that land-mine there was a long -- a bigger anti-tank mines. And had we just lifted the stretcher, none of us would have survived. It is clear that there was intention there; that we, the entire team in that line of work, should be killed right there, on the spot. If you allow me, the burned bodies, we collected them. To this day they haven't been identified, and there is no method of identifying these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, I'm just going to mention a document number. And at this moment, I cannot use that document: 65 ter 23592. However, I'm going to ask you: What was your knowledge, in practice, having done the work that you were doing? Who was held as a POW, for example, in the Zenica prison? Out of the Serbs, that is.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's what created problems for us. Categorisation of prisoner of wars. In Zenica, Serb civilians received call-up papers in order to be mobilised into the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since they did not wish to respond to this mobilisation, then they would be convicted to one to three years in prison and then they were imprisoned. These were civilians, these Serbs. The federal commission offered them to us for exchanges as prisoners of war. We could not accept such an exchange because we did not have the mandate to negotiate about civilians, and in essence these people were civilians who were taken away from their homes and then, in a very strange way, they became prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When were they mobilised; could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I omitted a question. It has to do with Ozren.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The bodies of these people who were discovered in Ozren, how many were discovered?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Out of this last group of 64 missing persons, during 2006 we discovered only ten bodies. And let me just say one more thing: These bodies were exhumed by the federal commission, the Muslim commission, and the media portrayed them as killed Muslims. It was only thanks to my intervention and that of the investigators of the Tribunal that we managed to locate these bodies in Visoko. When DNA analyses were carried out, it was proven that they were Serbs. They were taken over. They were brought to Banja Luka. Part of this group wag identified and the bodies were handed over to their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there anything unusual about the bodies that were discovered by the commission of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, they were all tied using a telephone wire that the military use. It was their hands and feet that were tied together. Secondly, at first glance, it seemed that these were ten bodies. When DNA samples were taken, that is usually done from the head and from the lower limbs. When the DNA reports arrived, what was shown was that there were more than ten persons involved; that is to say, that the heads there did not belong to those bodies. Rather, to other people. Also, through post-mortems the mode of death was discovered. There were two ways. One was beheading, as the doctors established, in a single blow either with an axe or a machete. The second way in which they were killed was through many injuries sustained in the neck area using a knife, in the chest area as well, and there were visible wounds on the legs of these persons. These injuries were also sustained after sharp objects were used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if there's no dispute about crimes having been committed, why do we need all the details of what we easily accept have been horrible crimes. Why do we need all the details of that, which is not the core of this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We need this to show even after the war there is no co-operation from federal side and there were -- only ten bodies were discovered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What then? And if -- what's the relevance of that? Even if there would have been obstruction -- and I don't know whether the Prosecution takes the position that there was no obstruction at all. We're not interested primarily in whether there was obstruction in revealing information about crimes committed against Serbs. And by the way, the Prosecution does not dispute that such crimes were committed. Whether then there was an obstruction or not is really irrelevant for our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We think, Your Honour, with all due respect, that there is relevance, especially since still everybody is playing with the numbers. And we are laying a foundation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even that -- we have seen that -- Mr. Lukic, we've seen that in the statement. The witness has given lengthy explanations as how everything was exaggerated. We're not interested. We are looking at the evidence that comes to us - that is, how many persons were identified by DNA, et cetera, et cetera - and if no one tells us what was reported -- and again, the witness told us that it was exaggerated there, this was published. As long as that doesn't come to us, we're not bothered about it. It may bother, perhaps, the community. Not us, as Judges. We want to rely on concrete evidence specifically, and we do not need to hear what is wrong with all kind of publication and propaganda, perhaps, which we ignore anyhow. Let that be clear and please keep that in mind if you continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not propaganda, Your Honour, it's official. [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, official. Have you never heard about official propaganda, Mr. Lukic? Do you say that whatever comes from official sources -- the question is whether it needs to be corrected, because whatever official sources say, if it's here in evidence, you can, of course, challenge it. If it's not in evidence, even if it's from official sources, don't make any effort in contradicting something or challenging something which is not in evidence here. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, we have the burden of proof of executed people in Srebrenica is shifted to the Defence since the Prosecution never revealed or had the position how many people were executed, how many were killed in a combat operations. So since that burden of proof is shifted to us, we have to try to show by any means what we can prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm afraid that I strongly disagree with you, that the burden of proof is shifted to the Defence in relation to how many people were killed in Srebrenica. The issue, how they were killed, is a matter which apparently is in dispute in this case. The Prosecution takes a different position from the Defence. That is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And how many also is in dispute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore, we listen to the evidence carefully to -- we have updated reports exactly on how many bodies were identified through DNA, et cetera, and now you bring a witness who is telling us that there's all kind of exaggeration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not interested in exaggerated figures. I'm interested in the expert -- and that is, the Chamber's interested in the expert evidence presented here saying, "We found bodies there. This is what we found. We identified so many," et cetera, et cetera, and the whole case story with which this witness comes. I'm not aware that that cases story is presented as evidence to this Chamber, so there's no need to correct it. We rely on expert evidence presented by the parties on the matter, and we are not in need of any correction on matters which are not in evidence before us. Propaganda --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do have cases in this case as well. We don't have only full bodies. We have parts of bodies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And that's where we carefully look at, and we are very conscious that if a body is divided in three separate parts, that it doesn't make for us three bodies unless we know whether the bodies are identified by DNA, yes or no. And that's exactly apparently what this witness is talking about in his statement, and I just want you to understand what this Chamber considers to be relevant and what this Chamber does not consider to be relevant. If there is an issue about multiplication of bodies found by two or three, which is suggested by this witness in his statement, then, of course, the Chamber would not -- first of all, it's not presented as such in evidence. Of course, there are some -- some question marks open, and that's the reason why this Chamber very much focuses on what is clearly established and is not -- not taken away by all kind of exaggerations without a -- without having proper foundation. That's also the reason why this Chamber again and again and again takes the parties back to what facts are established. That's what is important for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, facts in this case is that finding of ICMP commission, and this gentleman knows how that commission works, and that's what we want to show. And we have the reason, and it's main evidence in regard of -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not discusses it. It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So if we hear from him, it will be much more clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. But then what I'd like you to do, Mr. Lukic, is that if you -- if he says there's exaggeration or it is multiplied by two or three, which is the suggested claim by this witness, then show it to us, put that to the witness and say tell us where the exaggeration here is, not they are exaggerating because that is not something we can consider. Take it. Let's see whether it's an exceptional, unique, exceptional feature, or whether this is generally applicable to what has been presented as evidence. I leave it to that for the time being. I think it would be good to take a break first. We will take a break. Witness, you may follow the usher, and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just summing up from before the break, the Defence bears no burden to prove anything, and nobody has shifted any burden of proof to the Defence during the entire trial so far, and nobody will do so for the remainder of trial. The burden that the Defence bears is to rebut the Prosecution's case, and that's all. We'll wait for the witness to enter the courtroom. No speaking at audible volume.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the witness comes in, maybe we could deal with one procedural matter. I was just warned by Ms. Registrar that I never mentioned the number of the video. So it's 1D05368, and we would tender that video into the evidence, only parts that are translated and -- actually, parts that are transcribed and translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And played, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We didn't play all of it, but there is a -- actually comments by Mr. Krcmar and the pathologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have to further discuss this in more detail, but I leave it to that at this moment. If it is relevant to understand the statement of witness, then of course it could be an associated exhibit. To the extent it is not, I think it should be then -- the proper selection should be made. I leave it to that for the time being. You may proceed. Yes, we can reserve a number already for the video or excerpts of it. Madam Registrar, the number reserved would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be D917.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that number is reserved for this video or at least the portions that will be selected. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krcmar, can I continue?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Sure we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 36 of your statement, you say that the identification process is almost at its end. You also say that the number of victims has been exaggerated somewhat. How many reports did the international commission issue so far?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. What is the system of reassociation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: This is putting bodies together and making them whole from a number of boney remains. Let me give you an example. For example, when two or three bodies are found on the surface, a sample is taken from each the bones. It is then sent to a laboratory, and then a report tells us how many donors the bones belong to. And when the report is received, a pathologist puts bodies together and actually makes sure that all the bones belong to the right bodies. It sometimes happen that a lot of skeletal remains are found and the pathologist cannot associate them with any of the bodies based on any of the forensic criteria. Such skeletal remains are marked with separate numbers and are thereafter referred to cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it would assist the Chamber if it would have concrete examples of what the witness tells us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the Federation, what is the difference between their method of work as opposed to the method of work in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Republika Srpska, we don't have the notion of cases. There's no such a thing as a case in forensics. It was first introduced by the Federation when the terrain was sanitized. According to what I know, in the Federation, there's about 7.000 of the so-called cases in respect of the bodies that have already been buried, and the number of 7.000 cases means that the bones have not been identified or associated with any of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at 1D5365.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While this comes up, I would like to put a question to the witness. In paragraph 36 of your statement, I read: "... the fact that the Bosnian side exaggerated the number of the victims ..." What exactly do you mean by "Bosnian side"? To which entity or institution are you referring here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I read here. Can you explain that, please. What do you mean by that? What exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until this very day, an official list of missing persons in Bosnia and Herzegovina, primarily Muslims, has never been published, unlike in Republika Srpska where a list has been made very public and transparent. Or that there is a law in Bosnia-Herzegovina which stipulates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You misunderstood my question. In your statement, you say that the Bosnian side exaggerated the number of victims. What do you mean by "the Bosnian side"? Tell me which entity, which institution, which person, did that? "The Bosnian side" is a vague description.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be very precise. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, headed by Mr. Muharem Sacirbey, presented information, according to which around 250.000 Bosniaks had been killed. We all know that this is not true. I'm talking about the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for the same paragraph, you said that that fact - that is, that there was an exaggeration - has been proven by the analysis of the list of Muslims who went missing in Srebrenica in July 1995. Now, where can we find that analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The analysis of that list is being carried out by my own institution, which is the republican centre for the investigation of war crimes and searching for missing persons. I hope that an analyst from my institution will appear before this Trial Chamber and do a better job than I could, i.e., would give you a proper explanation of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say that that analysis is still to follow. And, Mr. Lukic, I do understand from you that you will -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- present it at a later stage. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before us we have your statement. I just referred you to paragraph 36 where you talk about the process of identifying the actually missing Muslims. I'm now interested in 1D5365.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask for the document to be displayed on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see a document here. It was issued by the ICMP. The representatives of Republika Srpska, do they have any influence on the work of this commission?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: The representatives of Republika Srpska have no influence whatsoever on the work of the International Commission of Missing Persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you have an English copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was just informed that it was sent to translation. So I will be using only one table and I will read what we can see on this first page. This document must be in English but we didn't locate it. It says, and I'll read it in B/C/S -- first line is in English so I don't have to read the first line. [Interpretation] "Report on the analysis of non-identified post-mortem remains in the Sutina morgue in Mostar."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krcmar, did you ever warn the ICMP on the possible consequences of their way of work?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: I told them that before we have a list of all the missing persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was pointless to make a list of the bodies, especially bearing in mind the fact that this way of work adopted by the international commission would lead to a much higher number of unknown bodies than are actually held in the morgues in Bosnia-Herzegovina. According to their estimate, there is approximately about 7.000 such cases, whereas the actual situation is much different and the number is much lower. In that way, this gives rise to an exaggerated number of unknown bodies, creating a new group of unknown cases, or just cases as they with called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us how much lower it is? Is it 10 per cent, 30 per cent, 50 per cent? Could you give us a further ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I did not understand the first part of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said the number is much lower. Could you tell us how much lower the actual number is compared to what they present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The actual number of bodies in the morgues should not surpass 2500. This is a rough estimate on my part, but bear in mind that I'm familiar with the situation in the morgues. I've been involved in that work for years now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you ever put that on paper, your criticism, to what -- can we find that anywhere documented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not put anything on paper. However, I had some official talks with the international commission a few years ago and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a follow-up question. In answer to Judge Orie's question, you said there were about 2500 bodies in a morgue; but where you mentioned the estimate of 7.000, you are not talking about the morgue. Are you saying that the estimates of the ICMP are that 7.000 people were in the morgue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it is not about 7.000 bodies in the morgues. It is about their estimate, about 7.000 cases. A case is not a body. A case refers to a part of a body that has already been buried, as I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might be a bit more clear if we see the page 18 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Take us there, Mr. Lukic, and take the witness there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, mm-hmm. It is also in B/C/S only, so I will read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And before you continue, could you tell us from what year this report stems? Is it recent? Is it old? Is it from when?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's November 22nd, 2013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's relatively recent. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will read the part above the table. "Annex 2: Table of an estimated number of cases with regard to the known cases and the known unique profiles from the samples of bones in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This table gives the estimates of the number of non-identified cases in every morgue. It also lists the number of unique profiles isolated from the samples of the so-called case bones for which there's still no match or the match has not been found. "The cases in various facilitates, apart from KIP and PIP, are estimated based on the counting of body bags containing mortal remains. That means that one case equals one body bag containing mortal remains. For PIP and KIP, all cases have been subject to anthropological testing and DNA analysis, and they have been separated into individual bodies (T) and body parts (DTs). "As the situation is reviewed in every facility, as has already been done in Sutina, the actual number of bodies and body parts will be determined, as well as the number of body bags containing mortal remains, and those numbers will be added to columns 3 and 4." Mr. Krcmar, do you have anything to add? You can see the morgues where they are, what their sizes are.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: The -- four of these morgues are in Republika Srpska. The first one in Banja Luka. Then number 8, Sveti Marko in Miljevici. 11, the morgue in Nevesinje. I can't see the numbers, so I can't tell whether the next number is 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes, 12 is Djudjevak, Modrica. Let me just explain that under 10 the city cemetery Sutina in Mostar is where the bodies were listed, and we can see that, according to the first estimate, there were a total of 189 bodies. When the list was completed, when all the cases were analysed, they arrived at a number of 395 as you can see in column 10. Apart from the four morgues in Republika Srpska, there is 6.988 of the so-called cases elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that there were 6.000-plus cases in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: No, no, I meant in the Federation. Maybe I misspoke, did I? I apologise. I'm talking about the morgues in the Federation. When we add all figures together, we will arrive at a number of 6.988 of the so-called cases. Let me repeat that one case equals one body bag containing mortal remains. In that way, we are going to create unknown bodies, i.e., unknown cases, based on the mortal remains, and those will be receiving their judicial numbers. They will be buried as unknown persons. And the manipulation lies in the fact that prior to that, we never established the exact number of dead in -- or -- and missing persons in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this is where the manipulation lies in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could the -- could the columns, the titles of the columns, be read to us since the witness refers to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I think we were looking at number 10, which is about the Sutina Mostar. Could we know what the first column apparently presents. The title is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Estimate in number of unknown cases in 2012."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now the second column reads what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The second column where we see number 395 says [Interpretation] "Bodies/body parts after a review in 2013."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now the third column reads what?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where we see number 204, column is marked as [Interpretation] "Total number of cases buried in 2013." [In English] The next one, where we see number 125, reads [Interpretation] "Unique profiles -- unique DNA profiles which have not been matched in 2012." [In English] Where we read number 182, the column reads [Interpretation] "Profiles from bone samples which have not been matched, 2012." [In English] And the last column reads [Interpretation] "Remark."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what is the remark in relation to line number 10?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It reads [Interpretation] "50 per cent insufficient number of samples out of 395 bodies or body parts."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have up with question for you, Witness. Where is there a claim that all of those body parts represent individual persons that have died? Where is that claim? Because it's described here in terms of unidentified body parts. Apparently 182 DNA'd, or identified by DNA without a match. Where is the claim that these are individual persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, the claim stems from the situation that is there during the sanitisation and the exhumation of the bodies as I mentioned in one of my paragraphs, when, for example, ten bodies are found, how one acts in order to identify them and have them buried. In addition to these ten bodies, I think that the paragraph is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But where does this report claim that what is perhaps stored in the various body bags or what are parts, the ones who are not yet identified, whether that are all -- that every such a bag or every such a body part represents one person, because that would, if I understand you well, be the real exaggeration. Where is that claim to be found in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the second paragraph where it says "one case equals one bag with mortal remains."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you understand that to be that one case is one person, or is one case one unidentified small collection of bones or at least mortal remains. Where is the claim that that is one person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not stated specifically that it has to do with one person, but the Prosecution ordered that this bag already has a Prosecution number and will be marked as one NN body. One body that is unknown. So on the basis of these bone samples --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where did the Prosecution order what exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll see that document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see that document. Then we'll have to wait to see that. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We would offer this document for identification. Of course, we don't have [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... there's no translation yet, and we have seen only one page. Madam Registrar, the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be D918.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D918 is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can now see 1D5364. There is no translation of this document either since these documents were brought by the witness when he came to The Hague now, but it is order, and I'll read the introduction part. [Interpretation] "With a view to speeding up the process of identification and burial, as well as the rationalisation of the costs of preserving the mortal remains of exhumed identified -- identified in a preliminary fashion by way of DNA methods and unidentified war victims that are in facilities for preserving mortal remains, the Prosecutor's Office of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Special Department for War Crimes hereby passes an order ..." [In English] And not to read the whole document, we would need page 4 - obviously in B/C/S version - here. I'm sorry, we should go back one -- one page back. I just need to read introduction under Roman number IV. [Interpretation] What is written here is as follows. I quote: "On the basis of an analysis and the established state of affairs, the working group shall, for each and every individual case, regardless of whether it has to do with mortal remains or bags containing clothes, objects, footwear, and the like, compile a record with instructions for action that will be compulsory for all participants in the process of identification and burial in accordance with their authority based on the law." [In English] And under number 3, we need number 3 down there, and Mr. Krcmar will address cases under B and D under 3, so I will read. Under 3, it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you read the whole -- it's very short so that you start with 3 and then also clearly say where something is stricken through. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah. [Interpretation] "Unidentified mortal remains shall pertain to the following cases: "A. Beyond the mandate," and then we see that the institute has been crossed out. "B. From which it is not possible to isolate the DNA profile; "C. From which bone samples were not taken for DNA analysis; "D. From which DNA profiles were isolated but there is no matching." In parentheses, it says "(meciranja)." [In English] It's not B/C/S. It's some kind of translation of English into B/C/S. And under E: [Interpretation] "Mortal remains with less statistic probability." B is what Mr. Krcmar is going to explain to us first, what it means. And what is written there under B is as follows: "Mortal remains from which it is not possible to isolate DNA profile." "Mortal remains from which it is not possible to isolate DNA profile due to carbonisation, contamination, scarcity, or other reasons, and on the basis of opinions of forensic medicine experts shall, without delay, on orders from the Prosecution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, be buried under appropriate judicial markings, depending on the location of their exhumation." First bullet point: "At the cemetery from which they were exhumed, if possible, in the same graves, or in a separate plot within that cemetery." Next bullet point: "At the closest cemetery of the municipality on whose territory the mortal remains were exhumed outside the cemetery and in a separate plot."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krcmar, where do you see the problem in all of this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Well, precisely through this order, the way in which these cases should be treated has been prescribed. The ones that will be given their numbers. Bodies that do not exist, surplus bodies, then also when bodies had decayed, when they carbonised, when the DNA sample cannot be taken, or body parts when people who are identified had already been identified through classical methods. Let me just explain. Classical method is identification that was carried out until 2000, approximately, when we did not use DNA analysis, when people were recognised. There were quite a few of their bone remains left, and afterwards their families didn't have to give blood for DNA analysis. We saw in these tables that there were cases like this that will get the designation of NN bodies. On the basis of this principle, in this order, they will be buried in the municipality where they had been exhumed. For example, many bodies were exhumed in Srebrenica. People were identified, buried, but these surpluses will be buried some day as NN bodies and actually non-existent bodies. And it's not only Srebrenica but there were quite a few other municipalities where exhumations were carried out. So Tomasica, Zvornik, Kotor Varos, Sanski Most; all the places where exhumations were carried out. So, in this way, this number of reported case, missing persons without names, will be dealt with. So this is perfect manipulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one question. Again, where is the claim that what you call a case presents one body, one person? Because that's -- you say it is exaggerated because it may be that a few cases together would make only one person. Isn't that the gist of your logical conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are not my conclusions. We have to go back to the previous document where it says one case equals one body bag. And then the Prosecution issues an order, and we see that each and every one of these bags is going to be marked as one case and will be buried accordingly. I attended the registration of some of these bodies in Sutina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You say one case is one body bag. I do understand that and that apparently is how it was organised. Now, one body bag doesn't say anything about how many bodies are in there. Perhaps three body bags having only one person in it. Is that what you are explaining us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Reassociation and registration is done in this way. What you have asserted just now is what we managed to see in column 10. Out of the 190-something, I don't remember exactly, on the basis of reassociation, the figure of 300-something was reached. That is to say, it is correct that in one bag, there could have been mortal remains from several different persons. Through DNA analysis, one can realise that there are three different bodies there, but there is no matching. If you look at the family members who were donors -- so we have the bodily remains of three different men. Do you understand what I'm saying? In that way, three new bodies are created. There is not a single medical criterion that can say what is a body and what is a sufficient number of body samples to call something a body. Perhaps just one or more than that. There were situations when one single bone would be buried. When the DNA report comes in, we know who that is and the family accepts and then that one bone is buried because the family accepts that not more than that can be found. So on the basis of that, one cannot say that these three bones are not a body. Even one bone can be an entire body, if the DNA report is in association with that single bone or whatever number of bones one may have. I don't know if I've been clear on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I fully understand your explanation. What I have not found yet is where is the claim that there are so many persons. The only thing I saw in the previous table, I saw that at least 182, I think it was, DNA analysis were made or have been successful and that they could not be matched, which I do understand means that they are unique and that would support a conclusion that -- perhaps not 3- or 400 body parts would present persons, but at least for those 182 there's a fair basis to assume that these are 182 different persons which have not been matched to any other bodily remains. That is what I understand. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was only in this morgue that reassociation was carried out, in Sutina. This was not done elsewhere. It's just the international commission that said it was about 7.000 in 2012. We will see what the results will be, but they are certainly not going to be any less. It's only going to be more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please proceed -- yes, no, it is time for a break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I would like to ask the witness for one short clarification. On page 78 - it's no longer on your screen - lines 15 and 16, you said: "The Prosecution ordered that this bag already has a Prosecution number and will be marked as one NN body." When you here referred to "the Prosecution," you mean the Prosecution of BiH and not the Prosecution of this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes. Because Mr. Lukic had already read the order out, and it is from the Office of the Prosecutor of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, he read that out later, but I think that's now clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn for the day. We'd like to see you back on Monday, Witness, and I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way, to whomever, about your testimony, whether that is testimony you have given today or whether that is testimony still to be given on Monday, and we'd like to see you back at 9.30 in the morning on Monday. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day. We resume Monday, the 2nd of March, 2015, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 2nd day of March, 2015, at 9.30 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
